summary: A is materially closer to the frozen contract and has much better scope discipline. Both patches incorrectly duplicate FilesService.Add logic instead of routing Upload through Add, but B additionally makes several explicitly forbidden API and retry-layer changes.
reasons: A adds the exact required Upload signature and uses internal/multipartbody.NewFile with field name "file", producing a buffered, replayable body.
A preserves FilesService.Add implementation and existing FilesOption behavior, whereas B changes global Raw.Do body replay and ownership semantics.
B explicitly violates the contract by adding WithFilesFormFields and association-field multipart machinery.

B refactors unrelated retry behavior for all seekable request bodies and changes whether Raw.Do closes bodies, creating broad compatibility and concurrency risks outside the requested convenience API scope appears intended to cover through buffering plus Add reuse rather than transport changes). Both failed route through Add, but A's duplicate is localized and can be fixed easily to return s.Add(ctx, body, contentType, opts...). A's retry test validates multipart content on every attempt, whereas B only parses and validates Upload's body on second attempt.
risks_a: Upload duplicates Add's option handling, request construction, response decoding, and missing-data error instead of routing through Add as explicitly required.
Tests omit a failing source-reader case, despite the contract requiring verification that such errors propagate.
The retry test supplies bytes.NewReader as source content rather than a genuinely streamed/non-replayable source, so streamed-content buffering is not demonstrated strongly.
risks_b: Adds forbidden association fields and a new public FilesOption, changing FilesOption behavior and API scope.
Changes global retry machinery and caller/transport body-closing semantics, contrary to the contract and with effects on every Raw.Do caller.

Still duplicates Add rather than routing Upload through it, so core behavior remains split across two implementations begin contrary to the contract's maintenance goal). The seek-based GetBody implementation reuses one mutable io.Seeker across attempts; this is fragile if transports overlap body lifecycle or callers access the reader concurrently. Tests omit source-reader error propagation. Upload's retry test does not validate the first attempt's multipart body.
